Consequences: (1) every environment, including the test suite and CI, now authenticates as the production account, so any code path that calls `client()` and issues a charge will move real money; (2) rotating the key requires a code change and redeploy rather than a config update; (3) the previous fail-fast behaviour on misconfiguration is gone, so a wrong-environment run succeeds silently instead of erroring. Restore the `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (the `import os` removed at the top of the file needs to come back), and treat the literal on line 4 as compromised — it should be revoked and rotated at the provider regardless of what this PR ends up doing.

findings.title: client() behavior change has no accompanying test
findings.body: The client() function now sets acmepay.api_key from a hardcoded module constant instead of an environment variable. The only test-related addition in this PR is a fixture (fake_client) that returns a dict — it is never invoked by client() and there is no test asserting that client() sets acmepay.api_key to a particular value or fails without the env var. If this wiring were wrong (e.g. wrong key used, or the assignment silently dropped), nothing in this PR would fail.

findings.title: fake_client() return shape does not match client()
findings.body: `client()` in `billing/acmepay_client.py` returns the `acmepay` module object, on which callers presumably invoke methods (e.g. `acmepay.Charge.create(...)`). `fake_client()` returns a plain `dict` with a single `api_key` entry. A test that substitutes `fake_client` for `client` will not exercise the real call surface — attribute access on the dict raises `AttributeError` rather than asserting anything about the charge — so the fixture can only support assertions about the key itself. If the intent is to stand in for `client()`, return an object exposing the same attributes the production callers use.

findings.title: tenant_of returns an unauthenticated, caller-forgeable tenant id
findings.body:
`tenant_of` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`, so the returned `tenant_id` comes from a payload nobody has checked — expiry, issuer and signature are all skipped. Anyone who can craft a base64 blob can set `tenant_id` to any value, and the two functions in this file will disagree about the same token: `claims_for` (line 7) rejects a forged token while `tenant_of` happily returns its tenant. Any code that uses `tenant_of` to scope a query or an authorization decision is scoping it on attacker input.

Fix by deriving the tenant from the verified claims, e.g. `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]` (or `.get("tenant_id")`), which reuses the existing `public_key()`/RS256 verification path and avoids the second decode entirely. If the motivation was avoiding the key-store round-trip, cache `public_key()` rather than skipping verification.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from a JWT with signature verification disabled

findings.title: tenant_of() name doesn't signal it skips signature verification
findings.body: claims_for() (line 6-7) verifies the JWT signature before returning claims. The new tenant_of() (lines 10-12) explicitly disables verification (verify_signature: False) but is named identically in style to the verified function, with no docstring or naming cue (e.g. unverified_tenant_of) indicating the trust difference. A caller unfamiliar with the implementation could reasonably assume tenant_of() returns a value with the same trust guarantees as claims_for(), since nothing in the name or signature suggests otherwise, and then use the returned tenant_id for authorization or tenant-scoping decisions.

findings.title: No test exercises tenant_of()'s unverified decode behavior
findings.body: tenant_of() decodes the token without signature verification and extracts tenant_id. There is no test in this diff covering it, so a change that broke extraction (e.g. wrong key name, exception on missing claim, or accidentally switching to verified decode which would then reject tokens signed with a different-than-expected key) would go unnoticed. Since this function's whole purpose is to skip verification, any test should at minimum assert that a token with an unexpected/missing tenant_id claim or unverifiable signature still returns the correct value, distinguishing it from claims_for.

findings.title: Missing tenant_id claim raises KeyError instead of a handled result
findings.body: `unverified["tenant_id"]` assumes the claim is always present. A structurally valid token issued without `tenant_id` (or with a differently named claim) makes this raise `KeyError`, which is not an auth-shaped error and will likely surface as a 500 rather than a 401/403. Use `.get("tenant_id")` and handle the `None` case explicitly, or raise the module's own auth error so callers can distinguish "no tenant" from an internal fault.

findings.title: update_payment_method mutates object without ownership check
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm` from the caller-supplied `pm_id` (line 12) and writes `body["billing_name"]` to it (line 13) then persists it (line 14), with no `require_owner(user, pm)` call. The `user` returned on line 11 is fetched and then never used, which is itself the tell that the check was dropped.

Adversary: any user who can authenticate to the API. What they control: the `pm_id` path/query parameter and the `billing_name` field of the request body. What they get: the ability to enumerate or guess other users' payment method ids and rewrite the billing name on any of them — cross-tenant write, plus the response on line 15 returns `pm.to_dict()`, disclosing the victim's payment method record back to the attacker.

Fix: add `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after line 12, matching the read path on line 6:

```python
user = current_user(request)
pm = PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)
require_owner(user, pm)
pm.billing_name = body["billing_name"]
```

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unguarded body key and possibly-missing PaymentMethod

findings.title: No test would catch missing ownership check on update_payment_method
findings.body: update_payment_method fetches the user and the payment method but never calls require_owner before mutating and saving it, unlike the sibling read function on lines 5-7 which does call require_owner. Since no test exists for this new function, a cross-user update (user A updating user B's payment method) would silently succeed and nothing in the test suite would fail to reveal it.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from unauthenticated password reset endpoint
findings.body:
`request_reset` is the password-reset entry point and previously carried `@rate_limit("5/hour")`. With the decorator and its import removed, nothing in this function bounds how often it may be called.

Adversary: any unauthenticated remote caller. What they control: the `email` argument and the request rate. What they get: (a) unbounded reset emails to a victim address — mailbox flooding that can bury legitimate mail and is a common precursor to social-engineering the reset flow; (b) unbounded reset-token generation for a chosen account, which multiplies the number of live tokens an attacker can try to guess or intercept; (c) if the response or timing differs for known vs. unknown addresses, a free account-enumeration oracle at full speed; (d) direct cost/reputation damage on the mail provider account.

The PR rationale — "the email provider already throttles" — does not cover these. Provider-side throttling is typically per-sending-account or per-recipient delivery volume; it does not stop enumeration (which only needs the HTTP response, not delivery), does not stop token minting, and does not stop an attacker spreading requests across many recipient addresses. Provider throttling also fails closed on *your* sending reputation rather than on the attacker.

Recommendation: keep a limiter at this endpoint, keyed on both source IP and the submitted `email`, so one address cannot be targeted from many sources nor many addresses probed from one source. If the intent was to relax the limit rather than remove it, raise the quota instead of dropping the decorator.

findings.title: Handler reports success even when provider-side throttling rejects the send
findings.body: The justification for dropping the local limiter is that the email provider throttles. That moves the throttling decision from a local decorator (which short-circuited before any work) to the provider call on line 2. `send_reset_email(email)` has no result check and no try/except, and line 3 returns `{"sent": True}` unconditionally. If the provider now rejects or drops throttled requests \u2014 which is exactly the mechanism this PR is relying on \u2014 the caller is told the mail was sent when it was not, and the failure is invisible in the response. If provider throttling is genuinely the replacement control, inspect the result of `send_reset_email` (or let it raise) and reflect a throttled/failed send in the returned payload rather than hard-coding `True`.

findings.title: No test guards against reintroducing/removing rate limiting on reset endpoint
findings.body: The decorator removal changes externally observable behavior (request_reset can now be called without hourly throttling). No test file is included in this diff, and no repository context was retrieved showing an existing test that asserted the rate-limit behavior. If this removal is wrong, nothing in the given diff would catch it — there is no test exercising request_reset's throttling behavior before or after this change.

findings.title: Preview path skips _confined(), allowing arbitrary file reads
findings.body:
`read_export_preview` builds its path with `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` while the existing download path on line 14 goes through `_confined(name)`. `os.path.join` does not constrain the result: a `name` of `../../etc/passwd` resolves outside `EXPORT_ROOT`, and an absolute `name` such as `/etc/passwd` discards `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely, so the first 4096 bytes of any readable file are returned to the caller. The PR description says the preview "reuses the same layout as download", which is exactly what is not happening here. Replace line 20 with `path = _confined(name)` so both entry points share one containment check.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Preview path skips _confined(), allowing arbitrary file read

findings.title: No test coverage for new preview function's path handling
findings.body: read_export_preview builds its path via os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) directly, unlike the sibling function above which calls _confined(name). No test exercises this function, so a regression (e.g. a caller passing '../' in name) would not be caught. Add a test that asserts read_export_preview rejects or confines traversal attempts, mirroring whatever behavior _confined enforces for the download path.

findings.title: PR description says preview reuses download's layout, but it does not
findings.body: The PR description states 'Preview path reuses the same layout as download,' but `read_export_preview` builds its path with a raw `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` while the download function above it calls `_confined(name)` first. These are not the same layout — one path goes through a confinement/sanitization step and the other does not. A reviewer or caller relying on the stated claim would wrongly assume the same safety guarantees apply to both functions.

findings.title: Tenant ownership check removed from bulk_export (cross-tenant IDOR)
findings.body:
`bulk_export` now fetches every `Report` named in the caller-supplied `report_ids` and serialises it with no authorisation step. The adversary is any authenticated user (the PR description explicitly relies on authentication alone); what they control is the `report_ids` list taken off the request; what they get is the full `to_dict()` contents of any other tenant's reports, in bulk, by enumerating or guessing IDs. `api/auth.require_owner` documents exactly this requirement: "Every object read or mutation of another tenant's data must go through this."

Restore the check. If the loop was the performance problem, keep the invariant and move it into the query — e.g. fetch with a `tenant_id == user.tenant_id` filter and reject (or omit) any requested ID that does not come back — rather than dropping it. Authentication is not authorisation.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ bulk_export no longer verifies report ownership before returning data

findings.title: No test guards cross-tenant access on bulk_export
findings.body: The removal of the require_owner loop means bulk_export now returns reports regardless of tenant ownership. If any test suite exists for this endpoint, it would need a case asserting that a user cannot fetch another tenant's report_ids and get their data back — otherwise this regression (or any future reintroduction of the bug) ships silently. No such test is present in this diff.

findings.title: search_customers interpolates values instead of passing params to execute
findings.body:
`execute(sql, params=None)` is documented as "Run a parameterised query. `params` must carry every caller value." `search_customers` ignores that: it folds `term` and `status` directly into the SQL text and then calls `execute(sql)` with no params, unlike `get_customer` on line 5 which correctly passes `(customer_id,)` against a `%s` placeholder.

Beyond the obvious injection exposure, this is plainly wrong for reachable, non-malicious input:
- A name with an apostrophe (`O'Brien`) terminates the literal and raises a SQL syntax error.
- `term` containing `%` or `_` is silently treated as a LIKE wildcard rather than a literal.
- `None` for either argument stringifies to the literal `'None'` instead of matching nothing / being rejected.

Fix by matching the existing style: `execute("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s", (f"%{term}%", status))`, and decide explicitly what a `None`/empty `term` or `status` should mean before building the pattern.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` interpolates `term` and `status` straight into the SQL string and then calls `execute(sql)` with no params. Anything that reaches these arguments is parsed as SQL: a `status` value of `x' OR '1'='1` returns the whole customers table, and `x'; DROP TABLE customers; --` or a `UNION SELECT` payload reads or destroys data outside the customer scope the caller was entitled to.

Fix by keeping the value out of the statement, e.g.:

    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))

Note the wildcards belong in the parameter value, not the SQL text. If `term` should not allow user-supplied `%`/`_` wildcards, escape them before binding.

findings.title: verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS invariant enforced above
findings.body:
The existing send path immediately above parses the destination and rejects anything whose host is not in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` before issuing a request. `verify_endpoint` takes a caller-supplied `url` and passes it straight to `requests.get` with no such check, so the module's stated invariant — outbound requests only go to allowlisted hosts — no longer holds for any caller that reaches this function. Since the feature description says tenants register the URL, this is attacker-controlled input reaching an outbound fetch: internal services and cloud metadata endpoints become reachable, and the returned status code leaks the result back to the caller. Route this through the same host validation used on lines 8-9 (and disable redirect following, since `requests` follows redirects by default and a permitted host can 302 to an internal one).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS check (SSRF)

findings.title: New verify_endpoint has no test and skips host validation
findings.body: verify_endpoint is a new public function that makes an outbound GET request to an arbitrary URL, but unlike the existing post function it does not check ALLOWED_HOSTS before issuing the request. No test exists in this diff exercising verify_endpoint, so neither the missing validation nor any future regression (e.g. someone removing timeout, or changing status handling) would be caught.

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of returning a status for unreachable hosts
findings.body: A function named `verify_endpoint` that returns `status_code` reads as "tell me whether this endpoint is reachable", but the common failure modes of verification — DNS failure, connection refused, TLS error, timeout after 5s — all raise `requests.exceptions.RequestException` rather than producing a status code. Any caller written against the return shape (e.g. `if verify_endpoint(u) == 200`) will get an exception on precisely the inputs it is trying to detect. Catch `RequestException` and return a sentinel, or document that the function raises so callers wrap it.

findings.title: verify_endpoint name suggests pass/fail check, but returns raw status code
findings.body: `verify_endpoint` returns `requests.get(url, timeout=5).status_code`, an integer (e.g. 200, 404, 500), not a boolean success/failure result. A caller reading the name `verify_endpoint` would reasonably expect a bool or an exception on failure, and could misuse it in an `if verify_endpoint(url):` check, which would be truthy for almost any status code including 404 or 500. A one-line docstring stating that it returns the raw HTTP status code would prevent this misuse.

findings.title: Customer-invoice bucket created with all public access blocks disabled
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket.invoices` holds customer invoices (bucket name `acme-customer-invoices`), and the companion `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all to `false`.

Adversary and impact: the Public Access Block is the last-resort control that makes a bucket un-publicisable regardless of what policy or ACL anyone attaches. With it off, (a) any principal that can call `s3:PutBucketPolicy`/`s3:PutBucketAcl`/`s3:PutObjectAcl` — a compromised CI role, an over-broad developer role, or a future Terraform change — can make invoices world-readable with no second check, and (b) `restrict_public_buckets = false` means an existing or inherited public policy is honoured immediately by anonymous internet users. What they get is customer billing PII.

Fix: for this bucket set all four flags to `true` (or simply omit the resource and rely on the S3 defaults / account-level BPA). If some narrow sharing is genuinely required, do it with a presigned URL or a CloudFront OAC rather than by disabling the block. Also consider adding `aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration` and versioning for a bucket of this sensitivity.

Separately: this bucket is not mentioned in the PR description, which only claims to add a public assets bucket for the marketing site. A sensitive, publicly-exposable bucket arriving under an unrelated description should be called out explicitly before merge.

findings.title: New invoices bucket disables all public-access guardrails
findings.body:
The PR is described as adding "the public assets bucket for the marketing site", but the code actually adds a second bucket, `acme-customer-invoices`, and attaches an `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` with all four protections set to `false`. Nothing in the change makes the assets bucket public that was not already so (lines 7–10 are pre-existing context; only the alignment on line 6 changed).

Setting `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` to `false` removes the account-level safety net for a bucket whose name indicates customer billing data: any later ACL or bucket policy — including one applied accidentally or by another module — will take effect and expose objects publicly.

If the invoices bucket is genuinely needed, either omit the `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` resource (so the S3 default/account-level block applies) or set all four attributes to `true`. If only the marketing assets bucket was intended, this resource pair should be dropped from the change.

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same HMAC digest as `verify_stripe` but validates it with `expected == header`. Python's `str.__eq__` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the signature an attacker guessed correctly, allowing a forged signature to be recovered byte-by-byte across repeated requests. Replace line 12 with `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` to match the existing helper on line 7.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook signature compared with `==` instead of compare_digest

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function has no accompanying test
findings.body: verify_acmepay is new signature-verification logic but the diff includes no test file. If the comparison logic were broken (e.g. always returning True/False, or comparing the wrong values), nothing would fail. Since this is authentication-adjacent code, a test asserting correct accept/reject behavior for valid and invalid signatures should be added.

findings.title: 500 handler returns exception text and full traceback to the client
findings.body:
`handle(exc)` previously returned a fixed `"internal error"` body; it now returns `str(exc)` plus `traceback.format_exc()` as the HTTP 500 response payload. Any client who can make a request that raises — malformed JSON, oversized field, an unexpected type, a DB timeout — gets back absolute source paths, module and function names, local frame context, library versions implied by the frames, and whatever the exception message itself carries. Exception messages are a common carrier of sensitive values: driver errors often echo the failing SQL or the connection string, `KeyError`/`ValidationError` echo submitted data, and some SDK errors embed tokens.

The operational goal is already met by the `log.exception("request failed")` on line 8, which puts the same traceback in the logs. Keep the generic body for the client and give on-call a correlation handle instead, e.g. generate a request/error id, log it alongside the exception, and return `{"error": "internal error", "error_id": eid}, 500`. If a verbose body is genuinely wanted for local work, gate it on an explicit debug flag that is off by default in production config rather than returning it unconditionally.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ format_exc() ignores the passed exception and needs active except context

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ 500 response body shape changed: new key and non-constant error value

findings.title: No test verifies the new error response shape/content
findings.body: The change to handle() now returns str(exc) and a full traceback in the response body, a significant behavior change from the prior generic message. No test file is included in this diff, so nothing asserts what handle() returns given an exception. A regression (e.g., reverting to leak even more, or breaking the response shape) would not be caught.

findings.title: Reset path hashes passwords with unsalted MD5
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives a password hash with a single unsalted MD5 pass. MD5 is computed at billions of guesses per second on commodity GPUs and, without a salt, precomputed rainbow tables recover common passwords instantly — so any account whose password went through the reset flow is effectively stored in plaintext-equivalent form. The module already has the correct primitive two lines above it: use `hash_password` (bcrypt with a per-password salt) for the reset flow too, and delete this helper rather than keeping a second, weaker path. If a verification counterpart exists elsewhere, it needs to migrate existing MD5 records (re-hash on next successful login) since the stored digests cannot be upgraded in place.

If, contrary to its name, this function is hashing a reset *token* rather than a password, say so — the fix is different (unpredictable high-entropy token, timing-safe comparison), but the current code is still wrong.

findings.title: hash_reset_password returns a format bcrypt.checkpw cannot verify
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), while the new `hash_reset_password` returns a bare 32-char hex MD5 digest. If both values land in the same stored password column, the verification path cannot be uniform: `bcrypt.checkpw(raw, stored)` raises `ValueError: invalid salt` on an MD5 hex string rather than returning False, so a user whose password went through the reset path will hit an exception (or a silent auth failure) at next login. Either make the reset path produce a bcrypt hash via `hash_password`, or make the storage/verification explicitly discriminate between the two formats. Note also that MD5 is unsuitable for password storage regardless of which column it lands in.

findings.title: New password-reset hashing path has no test coverage
findings.body: hash_reset_password is new security-sensitive behaviour (used presumably to validate reset tokens/passwords) but no test exercises it. If the implementation were changed or broken (e.g. wrong encoding, wrong algorithm, truncated output), nothing in the test suite would fail.

findings.title: checksum() loads the entire file into memory
findings.body: `fh.read()` materialises the whole file before hashing, so checksumming a large upload or log file scales memory with file size and can OOM the process. Hash incrementally instead, e.g. loop over `iter(lambda: fh.read(1 << 20), b"")` and call `h.update(chunk)`.

findings.title: pull_request_target checks out and executes fork code with secrets
findings.body:
This change creates a classic "pwn request". `pull_request_target` (line 4) runs the workflow in the context of the base repository, so the job receives repository secrets and a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with write permissions — unlike `pull_request`, which gives forked PRs a read-only, secret-less context. Lines 11–12 then explicitly check out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha`, i.e. the attacker-authored commit, and line 13 executes `./scripts/measure.sh` *from that checkout* with `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` exported (lines 14–15).

Adversary: any person on the internet, since anyone can open a pull request from a fork. What they control: the entire contents of the checked-out tree, including `scripts/measure.sh` itself and anything it sources (package.json scripts, lockfiles, config, etc.). What they get: arbitrary command execution on a runner that holds `NPM_TOKEN` (publish rights to your npm packages — supply-chain compromise) and a privileged `GITHUB_TOKEN` (push to the base repo, tamper with releases). Exfiltration is a one-line `curl` in the PR diff; the PR never needs to be merged or approved.

Safe options:
- Revert to `pull_request` and accept that forks do not get secrets (the stated goal — giving external contributors the size signal — works fine without `NPM_TOKEN` if the script can run unauthenticated).
- Or split into two workflows: an unprivileged `pull_request` job that builds and uploads an artifact, and a `workflow_run` job that consumes the artifact and holds the secret without ever checking out fork code.
- If `pull_request_target` must stay, do not check out `head.sha` and do not execute anything from the PR tree; run only base-branch code, and gate the job behind an explicit maintainer approval environment.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target checks out and runs untrusted PR code with secrets

findings.title: json.dumps key narrows accepted contexts and can collide keys
findings.body:
The old key `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))` accepted any context whose keys were sortable and whose values were hashable. `json.dumps(..., sort_keys=True)` imposes a different, stricter contract:

- Non-JSON-encodable values that were previously fine (e.g. `datetime`, `Decimal`, `set`, arbitrary objects, anything with a `__hash__`) now raise `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` from what was previously a working call. That is an unhandled exception on a reachable input for existing callers.
- Non-string keys are coerced to strings by the encoder, so `{1: "x"}` and `{"1": "x"}` produce the same digest and silently share a cache entry (wrong render returned). Mixed key types (`{1: ..., "a": ...}`) raise `TypeError` from `sort_keys` instead.

If contexts are guaranteed to be plain JSON-compatible dicts, add `default=repr` (or an explicit encoder) and document the restriction; otherwise consider keeping a structural key or use `repr`-based canonicalisation that preserves key types.

findings.title: No test covers non-JSON-serializable context values now raising errors
findings.body: The cache key used to be built via `tuple(sorted(context.items()))`, which works for any hashable value (sets, tuples, dates, custom objects with `__hash__`, etc.). The new implementation calls `json.dumps([template_source, context], sort_keys=True)`, which raises `TypeError` for any context value that isn't natively JSON-serializable. This is a real behavior change for callers passing non-JSON types, but none of the tests in tests/test_cache.py exercise a context containing such a value, so a regression here (or the fact that this narrows the accepted input type) would go completely unnoticed.

findings.title: New tests depend on module-level _CACHE being reset between tests
findings.body: `_CACHE` is a module global that is never cleared by `cached_render`. `test_different_context_renders_again` renders `("{{ a }}", {"a": 1})`, which is the exact same key already inserted by the first test in this file, so unless the `counter` fixture clears `render.cache._CACHE`, that call is a cache hit and `counter.renders` will be 1, not 2. The same coupling makes `test_key_is_by_value_not_by_identity` order-dependent. If the fixture does not already reset the cache, add an explicit `_CACHE.clear()` (or autouse fixture) so these assertions are independent of test ordering.

findings.title: Test checks shell=False but never checks argv structure
findings.body: `test_runs_without_a_shell` only asserts `spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False`. It never inspects `spy.last_call.args` (or the positional list passed to subprocess.run) to confirm the command was actually built as a list of separate tokens rather than an interpolated string. The whole point of this change is switching from a shell-interpolated string to a list of argv tokens; if someone later reverted `create_archive` to build a single f-string command (`"tar -czf ... "`) but forgot to flip `shell` back to True, or otherwise broke the list construction while leaving shell=False, this test would still pass even though the command would fail at runtime (or, with a different execution mechanism, reintroduce injection). The assertion should also check the composed args list, e.g. that `directory` and the constructed filename appear as separate list elements.

findings.title: Name allowlist rejects names that previously worked (dots, dates, >64 chars)
findings.body: `create_archive` previously accepted any `name` and interpolated it into the command. The new allowlist is `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}` matched with `fullmatch`, so common archive names such as `nightly.2024-01-01`, `tenant.acme`, or anything longer than 64 characters now raise `ValueError` where they previously produced an archive. This turns a working call site into a hard failure at runtime rather than at deploy time. Please confirm against the actual callers what name shapes are in use; if dots or longer names are legitimate, widen the pattern (e.g. add `.` and raise the length bound) while still excluding `/`, `..` and NUL. Separately, a non-string `name` (e.g. an int from a job id) will raise `TypeError` from `fullmatch` rather than the intended `ValueError`.

findings.title: `directory` is no longer word-split or glob-expanded now that shell=False
findings.body: With the old `shell=True` string, a caller could pass `"/srv/data/*"`, `"/srv/a /srv/b"`, or a `~`-prefixed path and the shell would expand/split it into multiple tar operands. With a list argv and `shell=False`, the whole value is passed to tar as one literal operand, so those calls now fail with `tar: ...: Cannot stat: No such file or directory` and `check=True` turns that into `CalledProcessError` — a new failure mode for callers that previously succeeded. If multi-path or glob inputs are part of the existing contract, change the parameter to accept a sequence of paths and splat it into the argv (resolving globs in Python via `glob.glob`), and document the change. Worth grepping the call sites before merging.

findings.title: `directory` reaches tar unvalidated while `name` is allowlisted
findings.body:
`name` is now constrained to `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}`, but `directory` is passed straight through to `tar` as an operand. Command injection is no longer possible (list argv, `shell=False`) and option injection is blocked by `--`, so the remaining exposure is scope of read: if any caller lets a user influence `directory`, that user can have arbitrary readable paths (`/etc`, `/root`, another tenant's export dir, or a symlink pointing there) packed into `/exports/<name>.tar.gz`, which is presumably then downloadable. Consider resolving `directory` with `os.path.realpath` and asserting it stays under an expected export root, and/or passing `-C <root> <relative>` so tar cannot escape it.

I cannot see any caller of `create_archive` in this diff or in retrieved context, so I cannot confirm the entry point is attacker-reachable.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion
findings.body:
This test calls render(Invoice(lines=[])) but never checks the result. It will pass regardless of what render() returns for an empty invoice (even None, an exception-free garbage string, or the wrong format), so it can never catch a regression in the blank-invoice case it claims to cover.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice asserts nothing

findings.title: Mock-only assertion never checks actual output
findings.body:
test_renders_line_items patches format_line and only asserts call_count == 2. It never checks that render() actually produced correct output containing the formatted line items. If format_line's output were dropped, malformed, or misordered in the final render, this test would still pass.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Line-item test checks only call count, not rendered output

findings.title: Failing tie-breaking test deleted with no accompanying rounding fix
findings.body:
The PR is described as "fix the rounding and drop the failing test that was asserting the old behaviour", but the only change in this diff is the removal of `test_rounds_half_to_even`. No implementation file is touched, so either (a) the fix is missing and the test was deleted to make the suite green while the old behaviour remains, or (b) the fix landed elsewhere and this test should have been *updated* to assert the new expected tie-breaking result rather than removed. Either way, `round_cents` now has no coverage for the exact-half input, which is the case where rounding implementations differ most (ROUND_HALF_EVEN vs ROUND_HALF_UP). Please restore a test asserting the intended behaviour for `Decimal("2.345")` (and ideally `Decimal("2.355")` to distinguish half-even from half-up) and include the implementation change in this PR.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Deleted round-half-to-even test has no replacement

findings.title: New exporter functions added without any tests
findings.body: csv_rows, csv_escape (csv_export.py), dump_streaming, dump_pretty (json_export.py), and margins_for, usable_width (pdf_export.py) are all new public functions with non-trivial logic (escaping rules, chunking, arithmetic on margins) but no tests were added for any of them. The repo already has a test file for the sibling function csv_header, showing exporters are expected to carry tests. If csv_escape mishandles quoting, or margins_for/usable_width computes wrong values, or dump_streaming chunks incorrectly, nothing in the suite would catch it.

findings.title: New test relies on real wall-clock time, not on expiry boundary logic
findings.body: `test_token_issued_today_is_valid` calls `issue_token()` and `is_expired(token.expires_at)` without passing an injected `now`, unlike the existing test which explicitly passes `now=`. This means the test depends on the real system clock at run time rather than deterministically exercising the expiry window. If `issue_token()` sets an expiry far in the future (the normal case), this assertion will pass regardless of whether the expiry-window logic is correct — it does not test the boundary at all, just that a freshly issued token isn't expired 'right now'. It also risks flakiness if run near a UTC midnight boundary, since `token.issued_at.date() == datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()` can fail purely due to timing rather than a real defect.
